cards.question: How does a spinlock differ from a mutex when the lock is already held?
cards.answer: With a mutex the waiting thread blocks and relinquishes the CPU; with a spinlock the thread keeps running and repeatedly checks (spins) until the lock is free or it gets preempted, burning CPU cycles.

cards.question: What are the three main problems the lecture identifies with using mutexes and condition variables directly?
cards.answer: They require careful, error-prone use of paired operations (forgetting to unlock, signaling the wrong condition variable); they lack expressive power (e.g. no built-in way to express priority or complex invariants, requiring helper variables); and they still need lower-level hardware atomic instruction support to be correct.

cards.question: What is a semaphore and how does it behave when its value is zero vs. nonzero?
cards.answer: A semaphore is a synchronization construct represented by an integer initialized to some maximum value. A thread that arrives decrements it and proceeds if the value is nonzero; if it is zero the thread must wait until another thread increments (posts to) it.

cards.question: How does initializing a semaphore's count control its behavior, and what value makes it behave like a mutex?
cards.answer: The initial count equals the number of threads allowed to proceed concurrently (e.g. 5 for five simultaneous producers). Initializing it to 1 makes it a binary semaphore, behaving exactly like a mutex.

cards.question: Who designed semaphores, and what do the classic operation names P and V stand for?
cards.answer: Semaphores were designed by Edsger Dijkstra. P and V come from the Dutch words 'proberen' (to test/try, i.e. wait) and 'verhogen' (to increase, i.e. signal/post).

cards.question: In the POSIX semaphore API, what do sem_init's arguments control, and what do sem_wait/sem_post do?
cards.answer: sem_init takes the semaphore variable, an initial count, and a flag indicating whether the semaphore is shared across processes or only among threads in one process; sem_wait decrements the semaphore (blocking if zero) and sem_post increments it.

cards.question: To make a POSIX semaphore behave exactly like a mutex for threads within a single process, how should sem_init's shared flag and initial count be set?
cards.answer: The shared (pshared) flag should be 0 (not shared across processes) and the initial count should be 1, so sem_wait admits exactly one thread at a time and sem_post is equivalent to unlocking a mutex.

cards.question: What distinction do reader/writer locks let a program express, and why is it useful?
cards.answer: They distinguish read (non-modifying) accesses, which can proceed concurrently/shared, from write (modifying) accesses, which require exclusive access — allowing more concurrency than a plain mutex when many operations are read-only.

cards.question: Name three ways reader/writer lock implementations can differ in semantics across systems.
cards.answer: (1) Whether a single read_unlock releases all recursive read_locks or each needs its own unlock; (2) whether a reader can upgrade directly to a writer or must release and re-acquire; (3) how lock state interacts with thread priority/scheduling (e.g. a waiting higher-priority writer can block new readers from joining).

cards.question: What is a monitor, and how does it differ from using mutexes/condition variables directly?
cards.answer: A monitor is a higher-level synchronization construct that bundles a protected resource, its entry procedures, and any condition variables together; the necessary locking, unlocking, and checking happen automatically on entry/exit, hiding pairwise lock/unlock and signal calls from the programmer.

cards.question: Where have monitors historically been supported, and how does Java implement them?
cards.answer: Monitors originated in the Mesa language runtime at Xerox PARC. In Java, every object has an internal lock, and methods declared 'synchronized' are entry points into the monitor; the compiler inserts the locking/unlocking code, though notify must still be called explicitly.

cards.question: What are serializers and path expressions, as alternative synchronization constructs?
cards.answer: Serializers make it easier to express priorities and hide explicit signaling/condition variables from the programmer. Path expressions require the programmer to specify a regular expression (e.g. 'many reads or a single write') describing legal interleavings, and the runtime enforces it.

cards.question: How does a barrier differ from a semaphore in terms of blocking behavior?
cards.answer: A semaphore initialized to n allows n threads to proceed before blocking further ones; a barrier does the reverse — it blocks all arriving threads until n threads have reached that point, then releases them together.

cards.question: What is wait-free synchronization, and what Linux kernel mechanism is given as an example?
cards.answer: Wait-free synchronization achieves concurrency without explicit locking/waiting by optimistically betting there are no conflicting concurrent writes, allowing reads to proceed concurrently and safely. The example given is RCU (read-copy-update), part of the Linux kernel.

cards.question: Why do all software synchronization constructs, even wait-free ones, ultimately depend on hardware?
cards.answer: They all require hardware support to atomically update a memory location — this is the only way to guarantee that a lock is properly acquired, state changes are race-free, and all threads agree on the current state of the synchronization construct.

cards.question: In the naive spinlock pseudocode (check 'if lock == free' then set busy, else spin), why is it both inefficient and incorrect?
cards.answer: It is inefficient because the spinning loop wastes CPU cycles. It is incorrect because the check-then-set is not atomic: multiple threads can see the lock as free simultaneously, all set it to busy, and multiple threads enter the critical section.

cards.question: Name three hardware atomic instructions mentioned in the lecture that can be used to build synchronization primitives.
cards.answer: Test-and-set, read-and-increment (or read-and-decrement), and compare-and-swap. Not every architecture supports every one of these.

cards.question: How does the test-and-set instruction work, and how is it used to build a correct spinlock?
cards.answer: test_and_set(lock) atomically reads the old value of the memory location and sets it to 1 (busy) in one indivisible step. A thread spins while test_and_set returns 1 (busy); the thread for which it returns 0 (was free) exits the loop holding the lock.

cards.question: Why do atomic instructions bypass the cache and go directly to memory on shared-memory multiprocessors (SMPs)?
cards.answer: Because with caches involved it would be extremely hard to guarantee that concurrent atomics on different CPUs, possibly operating on cached copies, are properly ordered and race-free; forcing atomics to hit memory directly creates a single ordering point, guaranteeing correctness at the cost of higher latency and coherence traffic.

cards.question: What are write-invalidate and write-update, the two basic cache coherence methods?
cards.answer: Write-invalidate: when a CPU writes a value, all other cached copies of that location are invalidated, forcing future reads elsewhere to fetch from memory. Write-update: when a CPU writes, the hardware propagates the new value to update all other cached copies immediately.

cards.question: What are the three performance objectives for a good spinlock design, per Anderson's paper?
cards.answer: Low latency (acquire a free lock as fast as possible, ideally one atomic instruction), low delay/waiting time (quickly detect and acquire a lock once it's freed), and low contention (minimize traffic on the shared bus/interconnect from both atomic references and coherence traffic).

cards.question: Why do the spinlock performance goals of low latency/low delay conflict with the goal of low contention?
cards.answer: Minimizing latency and delay pushes toward issuing the atomic operation as soon as possible and spinning continuously to detect a free lock immediately, but both of these generate more memory/atomic traffic on the shared interconnect, increasing contention.

cards.question: Why does the plain test-and-set spinlock perform badly under contention even on a cache-coherent machine?
cards.answer: Because the thread spins directly on the atomic instruction itself, every spin iteration issues a memory-bypassing atomic operation that goes to memory regardless of cache coherence, creating heavy contention on the shared bus/interconnect and delaying the lock owner.

cards.question: What is the test-and-test-and-set (spin-on-read) spinlock, and what problem does it solve?
cards.answer: It separates the check from the atomic: the thread first spins reading the cached value of the lock (no atomic, hits cache) and only attempts the actual test_and_set atomic once the cached value shows the lock is free. This avoids issuing atomic instructions on every spin iteration, reducing memory traffic while busy-waiting.

cards.question: In an SMP with N processors, what is the contention complexity when a test-and-test-and-set lock is released, under write-update vs. write-invalidate coherence?
cards.answer: Under write-update it is O(N): every processor sees the lock is free at once and issues one test_and_set. Under write-invalidate it is O(N^2): every attempted test_and_set invalidates all other caches, forcing repeated re-fetches and re-attempts across processors.

cards.question: What is the idea behind delay-based spinlocks, and what is the tradeoff between delaying only after lock release vs. after every reference?
cards.answer: A thread waits a bit before retrying after noticing the lock is free, so not everyone issues the atomic at once, reducing contention. Delaying only after release keeps latency good but can still cause bursts; delaying after every loop iteration also works on non-cache-coherent architectures but adds unnecessary delay when there's no contention, hurting the delay metric.

cards.question: Contrast static delay and dynamic delay strategies for delay-based spinlocks.
cards.answer: Static delay assigns a fixed delay (e.g., based on CPU ID times critical section length), which spreads out access well under high load but wastes time under low contention. Dynamic delay picks a random delay from a range sized by perceived contention (e.g. tracked via failed test-and-set attempts), adapting better but adding complexity and randomness-driven collisions.

cards.question: What is Anderson's queuing lock, and what core problem does it solve compared to test-and-set style spinlocks?
cards.answer: It uses an array of N flags (has-lock/must-wait), one per processor, obtained via an atomic read-and-increment ticket. Each thread spins only on its own private array slot, so only one thread at a time ever sees the lock as free — eliminating the thundering-herd effect where everyone notices a free lock simultaneously.

cards.question: For the queuing lock to perform well, what two hardware/layout requirements must hold?
cards.answer: The system must have cache coherence (so a thread can efficiently spin on its own cached array element), and each array element must be placed in a separate cache line, otherwise updating one element would invalidate the cache lines (and spinning) of other processors' elements too.

cards.question: How does the queuing lock trade off latency, delay, and contention compared to test-and-set-based spinlocks?
cards.answer: It has worse latency (the read-and-increment plus modular indexing takes more cycles than a simple test-and-set) but much better delay (the next thread is directly signaled via its own flag) and by far the best contention, since the atomic is issued only once per acquisition and spinning happens on separate, non-shared cache lines.

cards.question: According to Anderson's paper's measurements, which spinlock implementation performed best under high load, and which performed worst under light load, and why?
cards.answer: Under high load the queuing lock performed best (most scalable) because contention is minimized. Under light load the queuing lock performed worst because of its comparatively high latency (read-and-increment plus modular arithmetic), while plain test-and-set performed well since latency dominates when there is little contention.
